rows.source: HSE schools and education safety leadership
rows.verified: The school employer retains overall legal accountability for health and safety even where day-to-day functions are delegated.

rows.source: HSE schools and education safety leadership
rows.verified: School employers should implement proportionate arrangements for risks to staff, pupils and visitors and communicate significant risks and precautions.

rows.source: HSE schools and education safety leadership
rows.verified: Head teachers should follow employer policy, maintain communication and ensure staff have suitable training and competence.

rows.source: HSE schools and education safety leadership
rows.verified: School safety management should focus on real risks and practical controls rather than eliminating all risk or generating unnecessary paperwork.

rows.source: HSE schools and education safety leadership
rows.verified: Higher-risk school settings can include workshops, laboratories, studios, PE, vehicle movements, construction and adventure activities.

rows.source: HSE schools and education safety leadership
rows.verified: A sensible school system has clear responsibilities, proportionate documentation, staff consultation and practical solutions.

rows.source: HSE schools and education safety leadership
rows.verified: Competent school safety advice requires suitable skills, knowledge and experience and may come from the employer, trained staff or external support.

rows.source: HSE schools and education safety leadership
rows.verified: Educational risk management should enable opportunities, involve employees, students and carers and avoid blanket prohibitions.

rows.source: HSE schools and education safety leadership
rows.verified: School controls depend on age groups, curriculum activities, premises, equipment, pupils' needs, visitors, contractors and local management arrangements.

rows.source: HSE schools and education safety leadership
rows.verified: Education evidence is premises-, activity-, pupil- and management-specific and is not an exact parcel-level accident probability.

rows.source: HSE dangerous substances and explosive atmospheres
rows.verified: DSEAR requires employers and the self-employed to control safety risks from fire, explosion and substances corrosive to metals.

rows.source: HSE dangerous substances and explosive atmospheres
rows.verified: Dangerous substances can include solvents, paints, flammable gases, combustible dusts, pressurised gases and substances corrosive to metal.

rows.source: HSE dangerous substances and explosive atmospheres
rows.verified: Dutyholders must identify dangerous substances and assess the associated workplace risks.

rows.source: HSE dangerous substances and explosive atmospheres
rows.verified: Risks should be removed where possible or controlled where elimination is not practicable.

rows.source: HSE dangerous substances and explosive atmospheres
rows.verified: Controls must also mitigate the effects of incidents involving dangerous substances.

rows.source: HSE dangerous substances and explosive atmospheres
rows.verified: Employers must prepare accident, incident and emergency plans and train workers to control or respond to dangerous-substance risks.

rows.source: HSE dangerous substances and explosive atmospheres
rows.verified: Areas where explosive atmospheres may occur must be identified, classified and protected from ignition sources.

rows.source: HSE dangerous substances and explosive atmospheres
rows.verified: Fire and explosion prevention starts by identifying flammable substances, release potential, ignition sources and appropriate controls.

rows.source: HSE dangerous substances and explosive atmospheres
rows.verified: DSEAR controls depend on substance properties, quantity, process, ventilation, containment, ignition sources, zoning and emergency arrangements.

rows.source: HSE dangerous substances and explosive atmospheres
rows.verified: DSEAR evidence is substance-, process-, workplace- and scenario-specific and is not an exact parcel-level fire or explosion probability.
